My feelings are mixed on this.

On the one hand, 72% of the population shouldn't get to decide anything for the 2%. I don't agree with democracy, and to that extent I agree with the SCOTUS ruling. As posted below, lynching and mob rule is also democracy.

On the other hand, the 2% shouldn't get to decide anything for the 72% either simply because they're the underdog. I'm fine with the 2% having their rights, but it's not fair to demand anything of it from the rest of the population, and to that extent I disagree with the SCOTUS ruling.

I think if the 2% want to get married (or joined in civil union or whatever) at city hall in a secular agreement, FINE. However, the 72% should not be forced to accommodate this right by eg being forced to perform services. The same way we're not forced to recognize religion by observing traditions (such as passover or ramadan), all we have to do is to let the religious observe their own traditions without stopping them. Churches losing their tax-exempt status if they don't comply is going too far, and forcing them to participate in something they don't agree with. This goes far beyond simply allowing gays to marry and crosses the line into forcing others to participate in it.

TL;DR, If homosexuality was itself a religion, the whole country would now be forced to participate in their traditions (gay marriage), which is wrong.

My belief is that men marry due to external pressure, or foolishness. I'm more interested in why women want to marry. I've never been able to get a straight answer.
The belief that the other party is as fully invested (for the same reasons) as the man. Often that is not the case.

Religion, taxes, immigration, employment benefits, internal and external cultural perceptions, child custody, marrying into richer family, attempting to strengthen bonds due to fear of abandonment, to tie two families together, irrationality from hormones, commitment for the long and difficult process of raising children. Some of those can be expanded and I'm sure there are additional reasons.

And not all social pressure is negative, playing into existing social structure has its own psychological, monetary, and, well, social benefits. Also, many people appreciate commitment and stability for their own sakes. I may not be one of those people, but I can understand the attraction despite the costs and potential hazards for both parties.

There are specific legal situations where marriage is the logical thing to do, otherwise I don't really see why anyone would need to marry.

IMO, marriage is status and is an essential part of the high achieving man's man package. Men are supposed to acquire jobs, acquire promotions, acquire wives, acquire stable marriages, acquire children, then acquire respect and admiration. A not insignificant number of men have tied their self worth to the perceived quality of spouse they can attract and marry. They fall in the trap of seeking to secure a spouse that impresses others by being pretty, well educated, high family status, etc. Guess what? There are women that prey on that pattern of behavior. Just as daughters are encouraged by their mothers to seek men that want to be more equal partners, Fathers need to start having the same talks with sons and let them know they don't need the status of marriage. Strong independent man don't need no marriage to be a good spouse.

Well, you have to look at those contracts in the historical contexts where they originated. I know this is going to sound sexist as fuck, and it doesn't reflect what I think marriage should be. I am just explaining how it used to be seen, ok?

So, why would you sign a contract like that? Well, because marriage didn't really use to be seen as a contract between the man and the woman, even if technically and officially that is what it is. It used to be seen as an agreement between the bride's family and the groom. The groom wants a virgin (of course, remember, this is the 19th century) woman who has been raised in a reputable home who'll be a good mother for his children and take care of his household, etc. That is a very desirable thing, so if you have a daughter like that you're not just going to give her away. You'll want the suitor to make a strong commitment to your daughter. Hence the contract.

Another reason is to forge family alliances: "You want your sons to be our grandsons? Well, this is what it's going to cost you."

Of course, all of that is gone. Any man who signs that kind of agreement nowadays is a sucker (no offence intended who anyone under that kind of contract, perhaps you have your own reasons...)
